```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r setup}
library(ecoPortfolio)
```

`ecoPortfolio` computes the carbon metrics that TCFD and ISSB ask asset
managers to disclose, explains where a portfolio's carbon exposure comes from,
and stress-tests it against carbon price scenarios. The examples use the
package's **fictional** example portfolio and benchmark.

## 1. Put holdings in standard form

`climate_portfolio()` checks the data and computes weights from market values.
All monetary columns are in millions of one currency; emissions are in tCO2e.

```{r}
p <- climate_portfolio(example_portfolio)
b <- climate_portfolio(example_benchmark, portfolio_value = 500)
p
```

If your columns have other names, map them with
`columns = c(scope1 = "my_scope1_col", ...)`.

## 2. Core metrics

```{r}
waci(p)
financed_emissions(p)
carbon_footprint(p)
climate_metrics(p, scopes = 1:3)
```

* **WACI** measures exposure to carbon-intensive companies (tCO2e per million
  of revenue). It needs only weights, emissions and revenue.
* **Financed emissions** are the emissions the portfolio "owns", attributed by
  the share of enterprise value including cash (EVIC) held, as in the PCAF
  standard.
* **Carbon footprint** is financed emissions per million invested.

Two holdings have no emissions data, so every metric covers about 90% of the
portfolio. Always report coverage:

```{r}
data_coverage(p)
```

## 3. Where does the carbon come from?

A handful of holdings usually dominate.

```{r}
head(waci_contribution(p), 5)
plot_contribution(p)
```

## 4. Against the benchmark

```{r}
compare_benchmark(p, b)
plot_sector_intensity(p, b)
```

The portfolio holds fewer utilities and energy companies than the
benchmark, yet its WACI is higher. Attribution shows why: allocation effects
are small, but the materials companies it picked are far more intensive than
the sector average.

```{r}
a <- waci_attribution(p, b)
a
plot_attribution(a)
```

## 5. Carbon price stress test

`carbon_stress_test()` applies carbon price paths to each holding's
emissions. It reports the cost as a share of EBITDA (earnings at risk) and a
valuation shock, which capitalises the cost with a multiple. The built-in
`carbon_price_paths` are **illustrative only**; download official NGFS paths
for real analysis.

```{r}
st <- carbon_stress_test(p, pass_through = 0.2)
st
plot_stress(st)
```

Holding-level results show who drives the loss:

```{r}
h <- st$holdings
h <- h[h$scenario == "orderly" & h$year == 2030, ]
head(h[order(h$value_shock), c("name", "carbon_cost", "earnings_at_risk", "value_shock")])
```

## 6. Open emissions data from Climate TRACE

When you have no company-reported emissions, Climate TRACE publishes
asset-level estimates with owners. Sum them to owners, then match the owners to
your holdings by name. Many owners are subsidiaries, so use `aliases` to map
them to listed parents, and check the matches.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
assets <- ct_assets(countries = "GBR", subsectors = "electricity-generation",
                    year = 2022, limit = 200)
owners <- owner_emissions(assets)
head(owners)

holdings <- data.frame(id = c("DRX", "RWE"), name = c("Drax Group", "RWE AG"),
                       value = c(10, 15))
matched <- match_holdings(
  holdings, owners,
  aliases = data.frame(from = "RWE Generation UK PLC", to = "RWE AG")
)
matched[, c("name", "scope1", "matched_name")]
```

Asset emissions are physical estimates (roughly scope 1) for one country and
sector at a time, so they understate group-wide emissions. Treat them as a
screening proxy.
